explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus tells His disciples, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" He says it right alongside the news that the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. The clock is ticking, and Jesus is the one who names the days.

Pentecost is a real day in Scripture, and Acts 2:1 shows people gathered for it. It isn't the feast Jesus names here, though. He says, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" I'd say that's a hard one to guess if you never saw the calendar on the fridge.

The Feast of Tabernacles is in the Bible, and Leviticus 23:34 mentions it. But Jesus doesn't name it here. He tells His disciples, "You know that the Passover is two days away…" Keep that date in mind, because everything in this passage happens in the days leading up to it.

True. Jesus says it plainly: "…the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified." Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10), so He is talking about what will happen to Him. I think this one is heavy to hear, so let's let it sit for a second.

This one is true, and the text is clear about it. Jesus tells His disciples, "…the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified." Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). So He is telling them ahead of time what is coming for Him.

explanations.answer: Arrest Him covertly and kill Him
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says they "conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." Covertly means quietly, out of sight. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly: this is where the plot begins.

That's not what the text says they plan. Matthew 26:4 says they "conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." Nobody in that courtyard is talking about sending Him away. They are talking about arresting Him quietly and killing Him.

explanations.answer: Debate Him in front of the crowds
explanations.explanation: Debating in the open isn't the plan in this passage. The text says they "conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him." The word covertly means they want it quiet, which is the opposite of a stage in front of a crowd. The next verse shows what they are worried about.

explanations.answer: There may be a riot among the people
explanations.explanation: That's it. They say, "But not during the feast… or there may be a riot among the people." The plotters are looking at the crowd and counting heads. The text gives the riot as their reason and nothing else.

explanations.answer: The courts will be closed for the feast
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions the courts closing. The plotters give their reason in their own words: "…or there may be a riot among the people." It's the crowd they are worried about, not a schedule. Courts closing is a good guess, but it's not in this passage.

explanations.answer: Caiaphas will be busy at the temple
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the passage says Caiaphas has plans at the temple. The reason they give is, "…or there may be a riot among the people." Caiaphas is the high priest, and the plotters met in his courtyard. But their worry in this verse is the people, and that's the answer.

Yes, baker. The woman came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, "which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table." She doesn't just hold the jar out or dab a little. She pours it right on His head. Hold onto that detail, because Jesus will say what it means.

Close, but the text says head, not hands. Matthew 26:7 says she "poured on His head as He reclined at the table." It's an easy slip, since hands are where we usually put things like perfume. This woman goes straight to His head.

Shoulders is a fair guess, but the text says head. She came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, "which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table." The head is the spot the verse names, so that's where it goes.

Yes, baker. "When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, 'Why this waste?'" Indignant means they were upset about what they saw. They said it out loud, too, so Jesus heard what they were saying.

The text doesn't say they were amazed. It says, "When the disciples saw this, they were indignant…" Indignant means they were upset. Then they asked, "Why this waste?" That's a very different mood from amazed.

The text doesn't mention any tears from the disciples. It says they "were indignant and asked, 'Why this waste?'" Indignant means upset, not touched. The disciples are looking at the perfume and thinking about what else it could have done.

This one is false, and the details matter. The disciples say, "This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor." They don't mention the temple at all. Their idea is that the money goes to the poor.

Right, baker, it's false. The disciples say, "This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor." The money goes to the poor, not the temple. That's the whole reason behind their question, "Why this waste?"
That's the word. Jesus says, "Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me." The disciples are looking at the cost. Jesus looks at the deed and calls it beautiful.

Brave is a nice word, but it isn't the one Jesus uses. He says, "She has done a beautiful deed to Me." He says it right after asking His disciples why they are bothering her. Beautiful is the word He chooses for what she did.

The text doesn't call her deed quiet. Jesus says, "She has done a beautiful deed to Me." He is answering the disciples, who had just asked, "Why this waste?" So the word He picks is beautiful, and that's the one to remember.

That's backwards, baker. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." So it's the poor who will be with them, and Jesus who won't always be. This statement flips the two around, which is why it's false.

Right, it's false. Jesus says, "The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me." The statement on the card swaps the two. Jesus says the poor will always be with them and that they will not always have Him.

That's it. Jesus says, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." He connects what she did to what He told them two days before the Passover. I think that makes her deed even more serious than the disciples could see.

explanations.answer: Anointed Him as king of Israel
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." Pouring perfume on someone's head is a big gesture, so I see why the guess comes up. But burial is the word Jesus uses.

explanations.answer: Refreshed Him for the road ahead
explanations.explanation: That's a kind guess, but it's not what Jesus says. He tells them, "By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial." The text gives Jesus' own explanation, so we don't need to guess. Her deed was for His burial.

explanations.answer: Her deed will be told wherever the gospel is preached
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." She poured out one jar at one table, and Jesus says it will be told in all the world. And here we are telling it.

explanations.answer: Her jar will be paid back to her many times over
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't promise anything like a payback. He says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." The promise is that her deed will be remembered and told. It has nothing to do with getting the jar back.

explanations.answer: Her name will be written on the walls of the temple
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the temple walls in this passage. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her." The promise is about her deed being told, wherever the gospel goes. The text doesn't give her name, so I won't either.

True, and it's a hard verse to read. Judas went to the chief priests and asked, "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" He is the one who brings it up. I think this is one of the heaviest moments in the passage.

It's true, and the text is plain about it. Judas went to the chief priests and asked, "What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?" So the question comes from Judas himself. I think this is a heavy verse, so let's take it slowly.

That's the number. The text says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." Judas asked what they were willing to give, and that was their answer. I think this is a heavy detail, so I won't joke about it.

Twenty isn't the number in the text. Matthew 26:15 says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." It's an easy one to mix up, since the numbers are close together. The verse says thirty, and that's what the chief priests set out for Judas.

Forty is a little too high. Matthew 26:15 says, "And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver." The chief priests are the ones who set out the silver, after Judas asked what they were willing to give. The number the text gives is thirty.
